items.prompt: Why can two stars in the same constellation actually sit at wildly different distances from Earth, despite looking close together?

options.label: They only need to lie in nearly the same direction from Earth, not near each other in space
options.feedback: Our eyes cannot judge depth across distances this vast, so two stars along almost the same line of sight look like neighbours no matter how far apart they really are.

options.label: Distant starlight bends on its way here and lands in the wrong spot
options.feedback: Starlight travels in straight lines through empty space; nothing is bending it sideways into a false position.

options.label: Stars in a constellation are always genuinely close together
options.feedback: That would only be true if constellations were real physical groupings, and they are not — they are just patterns traced from Earth's point of view.

options.label: Our eyes cannot tell one star from another at all
options.feedback: Telling stars apart is not the issue; judging how far away each one truly is happens to be what our eyes cannot do.

items.ok_line: Same direction from here is not the same as near each other out there.
items.ko_line: What a constellation actually captures is which way you're looking, not how far away anything is.
items.exp_title: A pattern built from direction alone
items.exp_text: A constellation is simply a set of stars that happen to lie in roughly the same direction as seen from Earth. Because the human eye cannot judge distance across gaps of many light-years, two stars can appear side by side while one sits far closer to us than the other, and the pattern we see is really just a flat projection of directions, with all sense of true depth stripped away.

items.prompt: Why does a constellation's shape slowly change over tens of thousands of years?

options.label: Each star drifts through space at its own speed and in its own direction
options.feedback: Those tiny yearly shifts in each star's own direction are imperceptible on their own, but added up across thousands of years they visibly reshape the pattern.

options.label: Stars swap places with neighbouring stars
options.feedback: Stars are not trading positions with each other; each one is simply moving along its own path independently.

options.label: The stars themselves are physically shrinking
options.feedback: A change in a star's size would not shift where it appears in the sky. Position and size are separate things.

options.label: Earth's orbit slowly moves the whole solar system sideways
options.feedback: Earth's own motion around the Sun does shift our viewpoint slightly, but it repeats every year and snaps back — it cannot explain a change that keeps building over thousands of years.

items.ok_line: Every star is going its own way, just too slowly for one lifetime to notice.
items.ko_title: Look at the stars, not us
items.ko_line: The stars in a constellation are not standing still relative to each other, or to us.
items.exp_title: A pattern that never truly holds still
items.exp_text: Every star in the sky is moving through space along its own path, at its own speed, unconnected to its neighbours in the pattern we happen to see it in. From one year to the next that motion shifts a star's apparent position by an amount too small to notice, but stretched across tens of thousands of years those small shifts accumulate enough to visibly bend a familiar shape out of recognition.

items.prompt: Why do you see different constellations in the night sky in winter than in summer?

options.label: Earth's orbit around the Sun turns your night side to face a different direction in space each season
options.feedback: Night falls on whichever side of Earth faces away from the Sun, and as Earth moves around its orbit, that away-from-the-Sun direction points toward a different backdrop of stars.

options.label: Stars themselves migrate to a new part of the sky each season
options.feedback: The stars are far too distant for any seasonal motion of theirs to explain what changes; the moving part here is Earth's position, not theirs.

options.label: The atmosphere blocks different stars depending on the temperature
options.feedback: Temperature does not decide which stars the atmosphere lets through. What changes is which patch of sky is actually behind Earth's night side at all.

options.label: Earth's rotation speeds up and slows down through the year
options.feedback: Earth's daily spin stays essentially constant all year; it is Earth's slower yearly orbit around the Sun that is doing the real work here.

items.ok_line: A different slice of space lies behind you each season, as Earth swings around its orbit.
items.ko_line: Night is the side of Earth facing away from the Sun. What changes about that direction across a year?
items.exp_title: Facing a different slice of space each season
items.exp_text: At night you are looking outward from the side of Earth turned away from the Sun, and as Earth travels around its yearly orbit, that away-from-the-Sun direction sweeps slowly around and points toward a different region of surrounding space. Half a year later Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, so its night side now faces roughly the opposite direction in space, showing you an entirely different backdrop of stars.

items.prompt: Why do some constellations near the celestial pole never dip below the horizon, while most others rise and set?

options.label: They lie close enough to the point Earth's axis aims at that their nightly circle never reaches the horizon
options.feedback: The closer a star sits to that fixed point in the sky, the smaller the circle it traces overnight, and a small enough circle simply never dips below the horizon.

options.label: They are much closer to Earth than other stars
options.feedback: Distance from Earth is not what decides this; two stars at similar distances can behave completely differently depending only on how close each sits to the axis point.

options.label: They are brighter and so remain visible through the glow near the horizon
options.feedback: Brightness only affects whether a star can be seen at all, not whether it physically drops below the horizon during the night.

options.label: They do not actually move at all
options.feedback: Every star traces some circle overnight as Earth spins. The stars near the pole are not motionless — their circle is simply small enough to stay above the horizon.

items.ok_line: Close enough to the axis point, and the nightly circle never reaches down to the horizon.
items.ko_title: Think about the circle each star traces
items.ko_line: As Earth spins, every star traces a circle around one fixed point in the sky. What decides whether that circle dips below the horizon?
items.exp_title: Circles too small to touch the ground
items.exp_text: As Earth spins on its axis, every star appears to trace a circle around the fixed point that axis is aimed at. A star sitting close to that point traces only a small circle, tight enough to stay above the horizon all night, while a star farther from it sweeps a much wider circle that carries it below the horizon for part of each day.

items.prompt: Why can a faint-looking star in a constellation actually be more powerful than a bright-looking neighbour beside it?

options.label: How bright a star looks depends on its distance as well as its true output
options.feedback: A powerful star sitting much farther away can end up looking fainter than a weaker star that simply happens to be much closer to us.

options.label: Faint stars are always the youngest ones
options.feedback: A star's age has no fixed link to how bright it looks from Earth; distance and true output are what decide that, not age.

options.label: Our eyes see distant stars as brighter to compensate
options.feedback: Eyes do not boost the appearance of anything based on distance; a star's apparent brightness simply is whatever amount of its light actually reaches us.

options.label: The fainter star is being partly blocked by dust
options.feedback: Dust can dim a star, but nothing about being in a constellation guarantees that. The distance-versus-output explanation covers this pairing without needing to assume any blocking dust at all.

items.ok_line: Apparent brightness mixes true power together with distance.
items.ko_line: What you see as brightness on Earth is not purely a measure of how much light a star truly gives off.
items.exp_text: The light reaching Earth from any star spreads out and thins as it travels, so the same true output looks far dimmer from a great distance than it does from close by. A star that gives off enormous energy but sits very far away can therefore look fainter in our sky than a much weaker star that simply happens to be nearby, since what we actually see is a mix of true power and distance rather than power alone.

items.prompt: Why does a planet appear to wander out of a constellation's pattern over the course of weeks, while the stars around it stay fixed?

options.label: The planet is relatively near and orbits the Sun, so its direction from Earth keeps changing
options.feedback: Being so much closer than the background stars, even a modest sideways motion in its orbit shifts a planet's apparent position against them noticeably.

options.label: The stars around it are not actually real, only the planet is
options.feedback: The stars forming the constellation are just as real as the planet; the difference here is simply one of relative distance and motion, not existence.

options.label: The planet is somehow not affected by Earth's rotation
options.feedback: Earth's rotation carries the planet across the sky right along with the stars each night; that nightly motion is not what makes it wander over weeks.

options.label: The stars are too far to be seen moving, and the planet moves faster through space than any star
options.feedback: Raw travelling speed is not the deciding factor here — many stars race through space faster than a planet orbits. What matters is how much closer the planet is to us.

items.ok_line: Near and orbiting, so its direction from Earth keeps shifting against the far more distant stars.
items.ko_line: Both the planet and the stars are equally real. What differs between them is how close each one is to Earth.
items.exp_title: Close enough for its own motion to show
items.exp_text: A planet orbits the Sun at a distance that is enormous by Earth standards but tiny compared to the distance to any star, so as it moves along its orbit, the angle from which we see it against the background of stars keeps changing noticeably week to week. The stars themselves are so much farther away that any of their own motion is far too small to notice over the same stretch of time, so they appear to hold still while the planet visibly drifts past them.

items.prompt: Why might a star you can see tonight in a constellation no longer actually exist?

options.label: Its light takes time to reach Earth, so you're seeing it as it was when that light left, not as it is now
options.feedback: For a distant star, that travel time can be enormous, so what reaches your eye tonight may be light the star gave off long before whatever has happened to it since.

options.label: The star could have physically moved out of that spot already
options.feedback: A star's own motion across the sky is far too gradual to make it vanish from view within a human lifetime; that is not what's at stake here.

options.label: Constellations are redrawn slightly every year
options.feedback: The star's own existence, not how a pattern happens to be drawn, is what this question is really about.

options.label: It never actually existed; the light was created by our atmosphere
options.feedback: Starlight reaching Earth genuinely originates from a real star; the atmosphere does not manufacture that light out of nothing.

items.ok_line: Tonight's light is old news by the time it reaches you.
items.ko_line: Light does not arrive instantly across the distances involved here.
items.exp_text: Light travels at a fixed, finite speed, and covering the distance from a star to Earth takes real time, sometimes a very long stretch of it. What reaches your eye tonight is light that left the star that long ago, carrying a picture of the star as it was at that earlier moment rather than as it is right now, so anything that has happened to the star since then is not yet visible to you at all.

items.prompt: Why would someone standing exactly at the North Pole never see certain constellations, on any night of the year?

options.label: Those constellations lie on the part of the sky permanently hidden below the horizon at that latitude
options.feedback: Standing at that latitude, the curve of Earth itself permanently blocks the view of the sky near the opposite celestial pole, no matter the season or time of night.

options.label: Those constellations are only visible through a telescope
options.feedback: Visibility to the naked eye is not the issue here; the sky in question is blocked entirely by Earth itself, not simply too faint to see.

options.label: Extreme cold prevents starlight from reaching the ground there
options.feedback: Temperature has no effect on whether starlight can reach a location; what blocks the view here is the shape of the horizon, not the cold.

options.label: Those constellations only exist during the day there
options.feedback: A constellation's existence does not depend on the time of day; the true obstacle is that the horizon itself blocks that part of the sky at all times from that spot.

items.ok_line: The horizon there permanently hides half the sky, and it's always the same half.
items.ko_line: At any single spot on Earth, the horizon blocks part of the sky. Does that blocked part ever change at the poles?
items.exp_title: A horizon that never rotates through
items.exp_text: At most places on Earth, the spin of the planet carries different parts of the sky above and below the horizon over the course of a day. Standing exactly at the North Pole is different: the horizon there stays fixed relative to the sky as Earth spins, so it permanently hides the same half of the celestial sphere, around the southern celestial pole, while permanently showing the other half.

items.prompt: Why doesn't the age of two neighbouring stars in a constellation need to match, even though they sit side by side in the pattern?

options.label: A constellation only groups stars by shared direction from Earth, not by shared origin
options.feedback: Nothing about lying along a similar line of sight requires two stars to have formed together, or at anywhere near the same time.

options.label: All stars in the universe formed at the same time regardless of position
options.feedback: Stars have been forming continuously throughout cosmic history, and new ones are still forming now; formation is not tied to one single moment.

options.label: Stars age at the same rate no matter how they differ
options.feedback: How fast a star ages actually depends heavily on how massive it is, so even stars born together can reach very different life stages.

options.label: A constellation's stars are always siblings from the same birth cloud
options.feedback: That would only be true for a small handful of real star clusters; an ordinary constellation is just a chance alignment of unrelated stars.

items.ok_line: Sharing a direction from Earth says nothing about sharing a history.
items.ko_line: Remember what actually ties the stars of a constellation together — and what it leaves completely unconnected.
items.exp_title: Neighbours in the sky, strangers in time
items.exp_text: What places two stars in the same constellation is only that they happen to lie in a similar direction as seen from Earth, with nothing required about where or when either one actually formed. One star in the pair might have condensed out of its birth cloud recently, while the other could be vastly older, having formed in an entirely different, unrelated part of the galaxy long before.

items.prompt: Why does an entire constellation appear to move together across the sky over one night without its shape changing?

options.label: The stars are so distant that Earth's spin carries them together as if fixed relative to each other
options.feedback: Earth's own rotation is doing all the moving here; the stars are so remote that this single night's worth of their own true motion is far too small to notice.

options.label: The stars are all gravitationally locked to each other
options.feedback: The stars of an ordinary constellation are not bound to one another by gravity at all; they are typically unrelated and drifting independently.

options.label: A giant unseen structure connects them physically
options.feedback: There is no physical structure joining the stars of a constellation; the pattern is only a matter of shared direction, not a real connected object.

options.label: Wind currents high in the atmosphere carry the pattern along
options.feedback: Stars lie far beyond Earth's atmosphere entirely; nothing about atmospheric wind reaches out to move them across the sky.

items.ok_line: It is Earth doing the spinning, not the stars rearranging themselves.
items.ko_line: Nothing physically links the stars together. Ask what is spinning underneath you instead.
items.exp_title: The sky turns because the ground does
items.exp_text: As Earth spins on its axis over the course of a night, the whole dome of stars appears to wheel overhead together, simply because we are the ones turning underneath a backdrop that is, for a single night, effectively motionless. Every star's own true motion through space is real but far too slow to show up in a matter of hours, so the pattern keeps its shape while the entire sky seems to rotate as one piece.
